subtopicTitle: General relativity — equivalence principle, curved spacetime (overview)

cards.back: The Einstein Equivalence Principle (EEP) states that in any sufficiently small region of spacetime, the laws of physics are the same as in an unaccelerated frame in the absence of gravity. More simply, a uniform gravitational field is locally indistinguishable from a uniformly accelerating reference frame.

cards.front: Distinguish between the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP) and the Einstein Equivalence Principle (EEP).
cards.back: The WEP states that the inertial mass ($m_i$) and gravitational mass ($m_g$) of any object are equivalent ($m_i = m_g$), meaning all objects fall with the same acceleration in a given gravitational field. The EEP is a stronger statement, asserting that *all* laws of physics (not just mechanics) are the same in a uniform gravitational field and an accelerating frame.

cards.front: According to the Equivalence Principle, what effect does a gravitational field have on the path of light?
cards.back: Due to the Equivalence Principle, a gravitational field must bend light. If an observer in an accelerating rocket shines a light beam horizontally, they would observe it curve downwards. Since an accelerating frame is locally equivalent to a gravitational field, light must also follow a curved path in a gravitational field.

cards.front: In General Relativity, what is the fundamental cause of gravity, and how does it affect the motion of objects?
cards.back: In General Relativity, gravity is not a force but a manifestation of the curvature of spacetime, caused by the presence of mass and energy. Objects (including light) move along the 'straightest possible paths' or 'geodesics' in this curved spacetime, which appear as curved trajectories to an external observer.

cards.front: Define a 'geodesic' in the context of General Relativity.
cards.back: A geodesic is the path followed by a free particle (one not subject to any non-gravitational forces) in spacetime. It represents the 'straightest possible' path in a curved spacetime, or the path of extremal length (shortest or longest) between two points. In flat spacetime, geodesics are straight lines.

cards.front:
What is the primary role of the metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$ in General Relativity?
cards.back:
The metric tensor $g_{\mu
u}$ is the fundamental mathematical object that describes the geometry and curvature of spacetime. It defines how distances and time intervals are measured within spacetime, allowing calculation of the spacetime interval $ds^2 = g_{\mu
u} dx^\mu dx^
u$. It essentially encodes the gravitational field.

cards.front: Using the Equivalence Principle, explain conceptually why clocks tick slower in stronger gravitational fields (gravitational time dilation).
cards.back: Consider an accelerating elevator. If a clock at the bottom sends periodic light signals to the top, the top observer, accelerating away, will measure a longer time interval between signals (due to Doppler effect and increasing distance). By the EP, this implies that in a gravitational field, a clock lower down (in stronger gravity) will appear to tick slower than a clock higher up (in weaker gravity) to an observer higher up.

cards.front: How does the Equivalence Principle predict gravitational redshift for light escaping a gravitational field?
cards.back: Imagine a light source at the floor of an accelerating elevator. An observer at the ceiling, accelerating upwards, would measure the light to have a lower frequency (redshift) due to the Doppler effect. By the EP, this implies that light emitted from a lower position (stronger gravitational potential) will be observed to have a lower frequency (redshifted) when measured at a higher position (weaker gravitational potential), as it 'climbs out' of the gravitational well.
